1149.title: The encircling prayer
1149.hook: Celtic Christians drew a circle around themselves with a finger, praying for protection
1149.howItsDone: In the Gaelic tradition recorded in the Scottish Highlands and islands, a person in danger would trace a circle around themselves with a finger while praying for God's protection; some Christians today use caim prayers in personal and community prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, take, Lord, receive: the Suscipe, and the end of the Ignatian days. Your line was your love and grace are enough.

A finger, pointed out at arm's length. A person turns slowly in place, sunwise, tracing a circle in the air all the way around. Then they step forward, and tradition says the circle goes with them. That's a picture from the Gaelic Christian world of the Scottish Highlands and islands, and it begins a new stretch of this year's path: the Celtic way of prayer. Prayer close to the ground, to weather, to doors and roads and hearths. Today's word: caim. The encircling prayer.

Caim is a Gaelic word, given in English as a circle or an encompassing. The prayers that go with it ask God to surround a person: before and behind, above and below, on the right hand and the left. Some were said for oneself, some over a child, a traveler, a house. And notice what the circle is. It isn't a magic boundary. In the prayers, the circle is God. The person isn't building a wall; they're naming what's already around them. The Psalms already have the same picture. Psalm one hundred twenty-five: "As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people." The hills around the city become a picture of God on every side. Psalm one hundred thirty-nine says it more closely still: "Thou hast beset me behind and before, and laid thine hand upon me." Beset, hemmed in, but by care. The caim has a cousin you met on day one thousand twenty-three: the old Irish prayer called Saint Patrick's Breastplate, which tradition gives to Patrick. One stretch of it names Christ with me, before me, behind me, in me, beneath me, above me. Same shape: a person at the center, and Christ named in every direction. Why a finger? Because a gesture can carry a prayer when words won't come, in a hospital corridor, at a bus stop, beside a crib, without anyone hearing a word. And the prayers don't promise that nothing hard will happen. They name who is in the circle when it does.
screen: `THE CIRCLE IS GOD, NOT A WALL.`

segments.voice: If there's room, stretch out your right hand, one finger pointing, and turn slowly, or just sweep your arm around you, tracing a circle; then rest your hand in your lap. Name what's inside the circle with you: someone you love, a worry, the room itself. If you pray, say the psalm's line, thou hast beset me behind and before; if not, just sit inside the shape you drew.
Caim. A Gaelic word for an encircling: a gesture and a prayer that name God on every side of a person.
Your line: circled by god. The circle goes with you when you step forward. Same time tomorrow.

1150.title: Blessings for everything
1150.hook: Scottish Highland blessings, collected as Carmina Gadelica, for kindling fire, milking, sleep
1150.howItsDone: Some Christians today pray from Carmina Gadelica or from modern books of Celtic-style daily prayer, saying short blessings over chores, meals, journeys and sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, caim: the encircling prayer, with God on every side. Your line was circled by god.

Morning in a Highland cottage. Last night the fire was banked low, the embers covered over to keep them alive. Now someone kneels at the hearth with cold hands, uncovers the glow, adds fuel, and blows it back into flame. And while doing it, they say a blessing. Not in church: at the hearth, with the draft coming under the door. A collector named Alexander Carmichael went around the Highlands and islands of Scotland writing down prayers like that, and published them as Carmina Gadelica. Today: blessings for everything.

Carmina Gadelica is Latin for Gaelic songs. Inside are blessings for the jobs of an ordinary day: kindling the fire in the morning, banking it again at night, milking the cow, churning, weaving cloth, setting out on a journey, lying down to sleep. Carmichael heard them from working people and printed the Gaelic beside his English, polishing some as he went. Nothing is too small. The fire blessing doesn't wait for a holy moment; lighting the fire is the holy moment. The first letter to Timothy says it: "every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving: For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer." Brother Lawrence turned his cake for the love of God. These blessings go a step further and give each chore its own words. Paul writes to the Colossians: "whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus." Whatsoever. The Gaelic blessings take it at face value. Christ, Mary, the saints and the angels are invited into the cowshed, the kitchen and the boat. The fire at night is banked in God's name, so the house is kept while everyone sleeps. The milking blessing turns a cold dawn chore into a moment of company. A blessing also ties attention to the job; it's hard to scroll a phone and bless the milking at once. And something tender: work nobody thanks you for, done in front of someone who sees it. Carmichael's world has changed, but kettles, dishes and commutes are chores too. The hearth has moved, and the habit can move with it.
screen: `A BLESSING TIES ATTENTION TO THE JOB.`

segments.voice: Pick a job you'll do later, the kettle, the dishes, the laundry, the drive, and see your hands doing it. If you pray, borrow the words from Colossians, whatsoever ye do, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, and ask God's blessing on that job when it comes; if you don't, decide to do it slowly, with full attention, as if it mattered.
Blessings for everything. The Gaelic habit, written down in Carmina Gadelica, of blessing the fire, the milking, the road and sleep.
Your line: bless the fire. Lighting it can be the holy moment. See you tomorrow.

1151.title: Thin places
1151.hook: places where heaven and earth feel close
1151.howItsDone: Some Christians make pilgrimages to places such as Iona, or keep a small local place, a chapel, a shore or a garden, where they go to pray; the idea of thin places is used in Celtic-style spirituality and retreat work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gaelic blessings for every chore. Your line was bless the fire.

A man on the run sleeps outdoors with a stone for a pillow. He dreams of a ladder set up on the earth, its top reaching to heaven, angels going up and down. That's Jacob, in Genesis, fleeing his brother, a story first met on day three hundred sixty-two. When he wakes, he says: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." A bare patch of hillside had turned out to be a doorway. People who pray in the Celtic way have a name for spots like that. Today: thin places.

A thin place, as people use the phrase, is somewhere the distance between heaven and earth seems to shrink, where the veil feels thin. Some name Iona, the small island off the west of Scotland linked with Saint Columba. Others name a mountain, a shoreline, a ruined chapel, a back pew. This lesson won't claim an ancient source for the phrase itself. What's old is the experience. Jacob's words go on: "How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." Dreadful, in the old sense: full of awe. The gate of heaven, in a place with no temple, no altar, nothing but a stone. Jacob sets that stone up as a pillar, pours oil on it, and names the place Bethel. Here's a tension Christians hold. Psalm one hundred thirty-nine asks where anyone could go to get away from God's presence, and its answer is nowhere. So why would some places feel thinner? One way Christians put it: it isn't that God is closer there. It's that people are more awake there. Some places strip away the noise: wind, water, height, old stones, or a room where something true once happened. Jacob's own line holds both halves. The Lord was in this place, and I knew it not. The thinness was on his side. So a thin place doesn't have to be famous. A kitchen where someone you loved used to cook. A bench where someone heard hard news and somehow got through. A small chapel in the middle of the night.
screen: `THE GATE OF HEAVEN, AT A STONE.`

segments.voice: If there's a thin place near you, a window, a tree, a corner of a church, go there now or soon; if not, remember one, somewhere that seemed close to something more, and see it clearly: the light, the sounds, where you stood. Don't explain it; just go back. If you pray, say Jacob's words: surely the LORD is in this place.
Thin places. Places where heaven and earth feel close, like Jacob's stone at Bethel: the gate of heaven, found on bare ground.
Your line: heaven is thin here. A bare hillside was a doorway all along. Rest well.

1152.title: Wandering for Christ
1152.hook: Irish monks set out in boats without oars, going where God led
1152.howItsDone: Some Christians today go on walking pilgrimages, including to old Celtic sites such as Iona; others take the Irish idea of peregrinatio inwardly, as a way of holding their plans loosely and trusting God to lead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, thin places: spots where heaven and earth seem close. Your line was heaven is thin here.

Three men wash up on the coast of Cornwall in a little boat made of hides. The boat has no oars. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, an old English record, tells it plainly. They had slipped away from Ireland because they wanted to be on pilgrimage for the love of God, and they did not care where. They took food for about a week and let the sea carry them. Then they were brought before King Alfred, who must have had questions. Nobody had steered. That was the whole point. Irish Christians had a Latin word for setting out like this: peregrinatio. Wandering for Christ.
screen: `FOR THE LOVE OF GOD, THEY CARED NOT WHERE.`

segments.voice: In everyday Latin, peregrinatio meant living abroad, being the foreigner in town. Irish Christians gave it a sharper edge: leaving home on purpose, as an offering to God. Not a trip with a ticket back. An exile you chose. Some looked back to Abraham. In Genesis, God says to him: "Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee." No map, just a promise. Hebrews says "he went out, not knowing whither he went," and a few verses on calls the people of faith "strangers and pilgrims on the earth." Some Irish monks took that at its word. Columba, met back on day seven hundred eighty-eight, left Ireland and settled on Iona; his biographer Adomnán says he sailed away wishing to be a pilgrim for Christ. Others, the stories say, pushed out with no plan and let the wind and the current choose the shore. A boat without oars sounds reckless. To them it was trust you could see. Where they landed, the stories go on, they prayed, and some built a small community and stayed for life. Christians read this old practice in more than one way. Some hear a call that came to a few, and still comes, to leave everything. Some walk long pilgrim roads for a season. And some hear a picture of the inner life: holding plans loosely, and saying yes to the place where you've been set down.

Bring today's plan to mind and look for one small gap you could leave open: a different street home, a bench you've never sat on, a door you always walk past, without picking where it leads. Notice what happens in you as you loosen your grip on the oars, even a little. If you pray, hold the open space before God, the way Abraham set out.
Peregrinatio. Latin for living abroad; for the Irish saints, leaving home for the love of God and going where they were led.
Your line: where the wind takes. Plans held loosely leave room for a shore nobody chose. Until tomorrow.

1153.title: Morning and evening
1153.hook: the prayer book's two daily offices, morning prayer and evening prayer
1153.howItsDone: In the Anglican tradition, Morning and Evening Prayer from the Book of Common Prayer or a newer prayer book are said or sung daily in some cathedrals and parishes, and some clergy and lay people pray them on their own at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, peregrinatio: a boat with no oars, for the love of God. Your line was where the wind takes.

"Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice." That's Psalm fifty-five, someone in real trouble, hanging their prayers on the clock. In Exodus, too, one lamb is offered in the morning and another at evening, day by day. The day has two hinges: getting up and lying down. The Church of England's Book of Common Prayer built on them, with The Order for Morning Prayer and The Order for Evening Prayer, daily throughout the year. Today the Anglican way of prayer begins, with a door at each end of the day.
screen: `ONE LAMB AT MORNING, ONE AT EVENING.`

segments.voice: Day one hundred seven gave the daily office a first look; here's its shape in the old prayer book. Morning Prayer opens with lines of scripture and a confession said together, and soon comes a short exchange. The minister says, "O Lord, open thou our lips." The people answer, "And our mouth shall shew forth thy praise." Then psalms, an Old Testament reading, a song, a New Testament reading, another song, the creed, the Lord's Prayer, and short prayers called collects. Evening Prayer has the same bones, with its own songs and collects. The book lays out the psalms so the whole Psalter is read through each month. Now the last collect on each side of the day. In the morning: "O Lord, our heavenly Father, Almighty and everlasting God, who hast safely brought us to the beginning of this day." At night: "Lighten our darkness, we beseech thee, O Lord; and by thy great mercy defend us from all perils and dangers of this night." One says thank you for getting to the morning. The other, at the door of the dark, asks for keeping. Tradition says Thomas Cranmer, the archbishop who shaped the English prayer book, folded the monastery's many hours of prayer into these two, so a farmer or a shopkeeper could keep them as well as a monk. Psalm ninety-two already had the idea: "To shew forth thy lovingkindness in the morning, and thy faithfulness every night." Some Anglicans pray the full offices in church, some at a kitchen table, some only the collects. The length can change. The two hinges stay.
screen: `BROUGHT TO THE BEGINNING OF THIS DAY.`

segments.voice: In the morning, take the old opening line, O Lord, open thou our lips; in the evening, the night one, lighten our darkness. If you pray, let the line be your prayer for a while; if you don't, simply hold it and notice the hinge of the day turning.
Morning and evening. The prayer book's two daily offices, Morning Prayer and Evening Prayer: the two hinges of the day, both turned toward God.
Your line: morning and evening. Love at the start, faithfulness at the close. I'll be here tomorrow.

1154.title: Choral evensong
1154.hook: a sung service at dusk, with the Magnificat and Nunc Dimittis
1154.howItsDone: Choral evensong is sung by choirs in Anglican cathedrals, college chapels and some parish churches, usually in the late afternoon; people may join in the responses or simply sit and listen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, morning and evening: the prayer book's two hinges of the day. Your line was morning and evening.

The light is going outside a stone chapel. A few people sit in the carved wooden stalls: a student with a backpack, someone still in work clothes, a visitor who wandered in out of the cold. A bell, an organ note, and the choir begins. You can sing along if you know it, or just sit. The choir carries most of the singing: the psalm for the day, a song after each of the two readings, prayers sung back and forth, and then out into the dark. It's yesterday's Evening Prayer, set to music. Today's word: evensong.

The two songs at the center of evensong come from the first pages of Luke, and they belong to two people at opposite ends of a story. You've met both before on this path. The first is Mary's. She has just been told she will bear a child, and visits her cousin Elizabeth. There she says: "My soul doth magnify the Lord, and my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." Listen to where it goes: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away." Not a lullaby. A world turned over. In church it's known by its first word in Latin, Magnificat. The second song is Simeon's. Luke says it had been shown to him that he would not see death until he had seen the Lord's Christ. When Mary and Joseph bring the baby into the temple, Simeon takes him in his arms and blesses God: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation." Its Latin name is its first words, Nunc dimittis: now you let go. So evensong sets a beginning and an ending side by side: a woman carrying a child, singing about the low lifted up, and a man who has waited, ready to go in peace. Sung at dusk, Simeon's words can be heard as a word about the day itself. And these songs aren't only Anglican. Catholic evening prayer, Vespers, sings the Magnificat too.
screen: `A BEGINNING AND AN ENDING AT DUSK.`

segments.voice: If you can, play a recording of evensong, or just Simeon's song; if not, let one line come back by itself: now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace. Then let the day go, piece by piece: the meeting, the drive, the dishes. Listening can be the whole prayer, and if you pray, hand the day back to God in Simeon's words.
Evensong. Evening Prayer sung at dusk, with Mary's Magnificat and Simeon's Nunc dimittis at its heart.
Your line: the day ends in song. Mary's song lifts the low; Simeon's lets go in peace. Good night.

1155.title: The country parson
1155.hook: George Herbert on the pastor who visits, teaches and prays through the ordinary
1155.howItsDone: In parish life, Anglican clergy and lay visitors call on the sick, the housebound and the grieving at home, and some clergy still read Herbert's The Country Parson as a picture of a pastor's work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, evensong: Mary's song and Simeon's, sung as the light goes. Your line was the day ends in song.

A small book with a long title: A Priest to the Temple, or, The Country Parson. Its author, George Herbert, first met back on day eight hundred eighty-three, was a poet and a priest of the Church of England who served a small country parish. In short chapters he sets down what a good pastor does: how he lives, preaches, comforts, and runs his house. One chapter follows him out the door on an ordinary weekday afternoon, walking from house to house. Not on Sunday, when everyone is ready for him. On a plain weekday, when nobody is. Today: the country parson.

Herbert's reason for the weekday visit is simple, and a little sly. On Sunday, people come to church dressed up and on their best behavior. On a weekday afternoon the parson finds them as they really are, in the middle of their work and their troubles, and that's where he can actually help. So he goes from house to house: comforting the sick, praising the hard-working, admonishing the idle, giving to those in need, and, where it's welcome, praying with them right there among the pots and tools. The Bible behind this is plain. In Jesus's picture of the last judgment, the king says, "I was sick, and ye visited me." The letter of James puts it more bluntly: "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction." Herbert's poems say it from the inside. In one called The Elixir, he asks God to teach him to see God in all things, then lands here: "Who sweeps a room, as for thy laws, / Makes that and th' action fine." Sweeping. Not a vision, not a cathedral. A broom. That's Herbert's Anglican way: holiness in the ordinary parish, week and room. Not every Christian has a parson. Some have a pastor, a priest, an elder, a small-group leader, or a neighbor who simply shows up. But the picture travels: someone who knows the street, knocks on the door, and sits down at the kitchen table in the middle of the mess.
screen: `I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Let a face come to mind: someone sick, someone alone, someone you haven't sat with in a while. See yourself knocking, being let in, sitting down in the middle of their day, and ask what you could bring: soup, a card, an hour, or a call if a visit isn't possible. If you pray, hold that person before God now, by name.
